candidates.title: Can aid foster Africa's attainment of a just energy transition and external debt sustainability?
candidates.abstract_excerpt: 2-step system GMM on 39 African countries (2012-2022): net ODA correlates positively with renewable energy uptake but not fossil fuels; interest payments on long-term external debt negatively affect ODA; total external debt stock positively affects ODA received; notes ODA grants fell 8% while loans rose 11% (2021-2022), 'indicating reduced concessionality and worsening debt sustainability risks'.
candidates.why: Occupies the same conceptual space as P1 (aid, debt sustainability, energy transition, loans-vs-grants) with a quantitative panel-econometric approach, but is about continent-wide ODA aggregates, not the JETP instrument, and does not use the balance-sheet/DSA/utility-insolvency/currency-mismatch mechanism the manuscript proposes. Does not preempt P1.

candidates.title: Higher cost of finance exacerbates a climate investment trap in developing economies
candidates.authors: Nadia Ameli, Olivier Dessens, Matthew Winning, Jennifer Cronin, Hugues Chenet, Paul Drummond, Alvaro Calzadilla, Gabrial Anandarajah, Michael Grubb
candidates.abstract_excerpt: "Finance is vital for the green energy transition, but access to low cost finance is uneven as the cost of capital differs substantially between regions." Regional WACC differentials cut projected African green electricity output by 35% vs. models ignoring them; "a climate investment trap arises for developing economies when climate-related investments remain chronically insufficient."
candidates.why: Establishes the cost-of-capital mechanism central to P1/P4, but as a general modeling result (WACC differentials, no country/instrument specificity), not tied to JETP, sovereign debt ceilings, or utility balance sheets. Does not preempt.

candidates.title: Reducing the cost of capital to finance the energy transition in developing countries
candidates.authors: Matteo Calcaterra, Lara Aleluia Reis, Panagiotis Fragkos, Thibault Briera, et al.
candidates.abstract_excerpt: "Climate stabilization requires the mobilization of substantial investments in low- and zero-carbon technologies, especially in emerging and developing economies." IAM modeling with empirically-derived country-differentiated capital costs; reducing financial constraints yields joint climate and equity benefits.
candidates.why: Same cost-of-capital strand as Ameli et al.; complementary to P4's premise (concessional finance should lower cost of capital) but does not address debt-sustainability limits, loan/grant mix of a specific package, or JETP. Does not preempt.

candidates.title: Debt sustainability and climate financing
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Since COVID-19, public debt rose ~10pp of global GDP. Explores climate financing challenges (esp. adaptation) for SIDS/LDCs facing debt crises (rising rates, inflation); argues policymakers should combine concessional financing, debt restructuring, sustainability-linked instruments and carbon markets to reconcile growth, poverty reduction and climate action.
candidates.why: Directly on the P1 theme (debt sustainability + climate finance) at the global/SIDS-LDC level, and explicitly recommends concessionality/restructuring as the fix — implying today's instruments are NOT well matched to recipient balance sheets. But it is a general policy essay, not JETP-specific, does not analyze utility insolvency (Eskom/PLN/EVN/Senelec) or currency mismatch, and is grey literature (UNU-WIDER working paper, not peer-reviewed journal). Close to P1 in spirit but does not preempt the specific claim.

candidates.title: The Just Energy Transition Partnership Crossroads
candidates.venue: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (report), 20 Oct 2025
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Already known piece per brief; re-checked against the four propositions. Quotes: 'Far from the simplicity implied by headline announcements, the landscape of actual financial commitments is an extraordinarily complex assemblage of dozens of actors, each with their own priorities and operating procedures' — explicitly documents the P2 'jointly announced, severally owed' mechanism, but frames it as a coordination/implementation challenge, NOT a structural governance-design flaw. Notes SA/Indonesia/Vietnam JETP packages cover only 13%/20%/33% of sectoral needs and that 'bridging the gaps...will be difficult given existing debt burdens' but does not run a DSA/balance-sheet/currency-mismatch analysis (explicitly noted as a gap by the reviewing model). Mentions Eskom load-shedding as a political rather than balance-sheet constraint. Documents host-country frustration over loan-heavy financing and Indonesia's tactical exclusion of captive-coal emissions from targets (P3-adjacent) but does not develop recipients as strategic bargaining actors with exit options.
candidates.why: Touches P1, P2, and P3 all partially and explicitly names the 'severally owed' fragmentation (closest any source in this angle came to P2), but stops short of the structural-governance argument for P2 and the balance-sheet argument for P1, and does not develop P3's sovereign-agency argument or P4 at all. Does not preempt any of the four propositions as stated.

candidates.title: COP30 must tackle the debt trap and shortfall in public finance to deliver a Just Transition
candidates.authors: Bertha Argueta (Eurodad), Rebecca Thissen (CAN International), Claire O'Manique (Oil Change International)
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Argues sovereign debt burdens force Global South governments to prioritise debt service over health/education/climate spending and to keep extracting fossil fuels; cites that 70% of 2022 climate finance from wealthy countries was delivered as loans, deepening debt traps, with 50% of climate finance lent to SIDS/LDCs specifically.
candidates.why: General debt-and-climate-finance advocacy argument (grey literature). Does not mention JETP by name and does not develop the balance-sheet/DSA/currency-mismatch mechanism at instrument level — a general fiscal-space argument, not P1's specific claim.

verdict: P1 (balance-sheet non-absorbability) is NOT preempted as an integrated claim by anything found. Three adjacent but non-integrating strands exist: (a) quantitative aid/debt/energy-transition panel econometrics at continent scale (Nsakaza & Chilipaine 2025, peer-reviewed, Heliyon); (b) cost-of-capital/WACC modeling establishing a general 'climate investment trap' (Ameli et al. 2021 Nat. Comm.; Calcaterra et al. 2024 Nat. Energy; possibly Briera & Lefèvre 2024, unresolved); (c) global/SIDS-LDC debt-sustainability-and-climate-finance policy essays (Panizza 2025 UNU-WIDER; Eurodad 2025). None of these apply the argument to the JETP instrument specifically, none use the sovereign-debt-ceiling + utility-insolvency (Eskom/PLN/EVN/Senelec) + currency-mismatch combination as an integrated mechanism, and the one source that comes closest to the JETP-specific empirics (Csanadi & Helmeci 2025, Carnegie — already known) explicitly stops short of the balance-sheet framing. The manuscript will need to cite and position itself against strands (a)-(c), but P1 as stated appears open. P4 (solvency buys agency — the bimodal/two-tailed non-absorption argument) is NOT preempted anywhere found in this angle, peer-reviewed or grey. The general IPE literature on creditworthiness-driven bargaining power over conditionality (Fafchamps-type, NBER, JIEL) supplies the theoretical raw material but has never, in what surfaced, been applied to climate finance or JETP, let alone framed as a bimodal solvency effect emptying the loan instrument's domain of validity. Of the two priority propositions, P4 looks like the more clearly unoccupied and more novel claim. Caveat on confidence: OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar — the two broadest-coverage academic search APIs — were rate-limited for most of the session (OpenAlex for ~10.5 hours per its own Retry-After header), so this angle's coverage of the peer-reviewed literature is weaker than intended and should be re-run against those two databases before the manuscript team treats P1/P4 as confirmed-open. Two report-type candidates (Selvaraju et al. 2025 Grantham/LSE; Monsod et al. 2023 Climate Policy) remain substantively unread due to PDF/paywall extraction failures and should be manually checked.
